content.text: 🤿 Modal Verbs
🔁 Review
In our previous lesson, we explored helping verbs (be, have, do) and their crucial role in forming questions, negatives, different tenses, passive voice, and emphatic statements in English.
Quick Practice:
Identify the helping verbs in this sentence: "The documents have been prepared by our legal team."
Transform this affirmative sentence into a question: "She has completed the assignment."
Rewrite this sentence in the negative form: "They were discussing the proposal when I arrived."
🎯 Overview

Modal verbs are a special type of helping verbs that express modality—concepts such as ability, possibility, permission, obligation, and necessity. Unlike primary helping verbs, modals have unique characteristics: they don't change form for different subjects, they're followed by the base form of the main verb, and they don't use "to" before the infinitive.

The main modal verbs in English are can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, and must. Each modal verb can express different meanings depending on the context, making them both versatile and sometimes challenging to master.

We use modal verbs to express a wide range of meanings, including ability, possibility, permission, obligation, prohibition, necessity, advice, deduction, and future predictions. Understanding the nuances of modal verbs is essential for expressing degrees of certainty, formality, and politeness in English.
🏊 Can you do?
Match each modal verb with its most appropriate function in these sentences:
a. You must submit the application by Friday. b. She can speak five languages fluently. c. We might go to the beach this weekend. d. You should exercise regularly.
Functions: ability, obligation, possibility, advice
Choose the most appropriate modal verb to complete each sentence:

a. I _______ swim when I was five years old. (could/would/should) b. You _______ finish this report by tomorrow. It's extremely urgent. (might/must/would) c. _______ I borrow your pen, please? (Can/Would/Must) d. They _______ arrive late. The traffic is terrible today. (will/should/might)
Identify the function of the modal verb in each sentence (ability, possibility, permission, obligation, advice, etc.):
a. You must not touch that equipment. b. She could be at home now. c. May I ask you a question? d. You should see a doctor about that cough.
Rewrite these sentences using an appropriate modal verb:

a. I recommend that you take an umbrella. (advice) b. It is possible that she will join us later. (possibility) c. You are not allowed to park here. (prohibition) d. It is necessary for us to arrive early. (necessity/obligation)
🔍 Deep Dive
Modal verbs are powerful tools for expressing nuanced meanings in English. Let's explore each modal verb and its various functions in detail.
Can / Could
Can
- Present ability, possibility, or permission:
Ability
(having the skill to do something):
She can speak three languages fluently.
I can solve this type of problem easily.
Possibility
(something is possible):
Stress can cause various health problems.
Global warming can lead to extreme weather events.
Permission
(informal):
You can use my laptop if you need to.
Can I leave early today?
Could
- Past ability, polite requests, suggestions, or possibility:
Past ability
I could swim very well when I was younger.
She could play the piano by the age of six.
Polite requests
(more formal than "can"):
Could I borrow your pen, please?
Could you help me with this assignment?
Possibility
(less certain than "can"):
It could rain later today.
This policy could have negative consequences.
Suggestions
We could try the new restaurant downtown.
You could speak to your professor about the deadline.
May / Might
May
- Formal permission, possibility, or wishes:
Formal permission
May I come in?
Students may leave the room only after completing the test.
Possibility
(formal, about 50% certainty):
The director may attend the meeting tomorrow.
This approach may solve our problem.
Wishes or hopes
May you have a wonderful journey.
May all your dreams come true.
Might
- Possibility (less certain than "may"):
Possibility
(about 30% certainty):
It might rain later, so take an umbrella.
She might not attend the conference.
Suggestions
(tentative):
You might want to reconsider your decision.
We might try approaching the problem differently.
Polite criticism
(often in past form):
You might have told me earlier about the change in plans.
She might have been more careful with the equipment.
Shall / Should
Shall
- Formal suggestions, offers, or future plans (mainly used in British English):
Offers or suggestions
Shall I help you with those bags?
Shall we meet at 7 PM?
Future plans
(formal, first person):
We shall proceed with the investigation.
I shall return before sunset.
Formal rules or legal documents
The tenant shall be responsible for minor repairs.
All parties shall comply with the regulations.
Should
- Advice, expectation, or probability:
Advice or recommendation
You should exercise regularly.
They should invest in new technology.
Expectation
The package should arrive by tomorrow.
She should be here by now.
Logical deduction
The project should be successful if we follow the plan.
The results should improve with these adjustments.
Obligation
(milder than "must"):
Students should submit their assignments on time.
You should inform your manager about the issue.
Will / Would
Will
- Future actions, predictions, promises, or willingness:
Future actions or predictions
The meeting will start at 9 AM.
This investment will yield good returns.
Promises
I will help you with your project.
We will deliver the package by Friday.
Willingness
I'll carry those bags for you.
The manager will see you now.
Habits
(often negative):
She will talk for hours if you let her.
The printer will often jam when we're in a hurry.
Would
- Past habits, hypothetical situations, polite requests, or preferences:
Past habits
When I was a child, I would visit my grandparents every summer.
She would practice piano for hours each day.
Hypothetical situations
I would travel more if I had more time.
What would you do in my situation?
Polite requests
(more formal than "could"):
Would you mind closing the window?
Would you be able to send me the report?
Preferences
I would prefer to meet earlier.
She would rather work from home.
Must / Have to
Must
- Strong obligation, necessity, or logical deduction:
Strong obligation
(from the speaker):
You must submit the application by Friday.
All employees must attend the training session.
Prohibition
(in negative form):
You must not enter this area without authorization.
Students must not use mobile phones during exams.
Logical deduction
(strong certainty):
She must be exhausted after working for 12 hours.
It must be difficult to manage such a large team.
Have to
- External obligation or necessity:
External obligation
(rules, laws, or circumstances):
I have to renew my passport next month.
She has to work overtime to complete the project.
Necessity
We have to find a solution quickly.
You have to practice regularly to improve your skills.
Need / Ought to
Need
- Necessity (can function as a modal or regular verb):
Necessity
(as a modal verb, mainly in questions and negatives):
Need I remind you of the deadline? (formal)
You needn't worry about that. (formal)
Necessity
(as a regular verb):
I need to finish this report today.
She needs to improve her presentation skills.
Ought to
- Moral obligation or logical expectation:
Moral obligation
(similar to "should" but stronger):
You ought to help your parents more.
We ought to reduce our carbon footprint.
Logical expectation
The train ought to arrive on time.
This approach ought to work well.
Modal Combinations
Modal verbs can be combined with other verb forms to express more complex meanings:
Modal + have + past participle
(perfect infinitive) - Past possibility, speculation, or unfulfilled obligation:
She must have missed the train. (deduction about the past)
They could have won the match if they had played better. (past possibility)
You should have informed me earlier. (unfulfilled obligation/advice)
Modal + be + -ing form
(continuous infinitive) - Ongoing actions:
They must be waiting for us now. (present deduction)
She might be working late tonight. (present possibility)
He could be studying at the library. (present speculation)
Modal + have been + -ing form
(perfect continuous infinitive) - Ongoing actions that started in the past:
She must have been working all night. (deduction about ongoing past action)
They might have been trying to contact us. (speculation about ongoing past action)
You should have been practicing more regularly. (unfulfilled continuous obligation)
Modal Verbs in Reported Speech
When using reported speech, modal verbs often change:
Direct: "I can help you." → Reported: She said she could help me.
Direct: "You must finish this today." → Reported: She said I had to finish it that day.
Direct: "I will call you tomorrow." → Reported: He said he would call me the next day.
Direct: "May I ask a question?" → Reported: She asked if she might ask a question.
However, some modals remain unchanged in reported speech when the meaning doesn't change:
Direct: "You should exercise more." → Reported: The doctor said I should exercise more.
Direct: "They might come to the party." → Reported: She said they might come to the party.
Mini Dialogues:
Situation: Job Interview
Interviewer: Could you tell me about your experience with project management?
Candidate: Certainly. In my previous role, I would coordinate team activities and ensure deadlines were met. I must say that effective communication was essential.
Interviewer: That's interesting. How might you handle conflicts within a team?
Situation: Doctor's Office
Doctor: You should reduce your caffeine intake. It might be contributing to your insomnia.
Patient: I understand. Must I eliminate coffee completely?
Doctor: You needn't cut it out entirely. You could switch to decaf after noon, and you shouldn't drink any caffeinated beverages after 4 PM.
Situation: Business Meeting
Manager: We must improve our customer satisfaction ratings. The recent feedback indicates we may have issues with our response time.
Team Member: I would suggest implementing a new ticketing system. It could help us track and prioritize customer inquiries more effectively.
Manager: That's a good idea. We should explore that option. Can you prepare a proposal for next week's meeting?
Common Errors and Formal Variations:
"I must to go now." ❌ → "I must go now." ✓ (modals don't use "to")
"She cans speak French." ❌ → "She can speak French." ✓ (modals don't change form)
"You should to exercise more." ❌ → "You should exercise more." ✓ (no "to" after modals)
"I will can help you tomorrow." ❌ → "I will be able to help you tomorrow." ✓ (don't use two modals together)
"You may proceed with the project." (formal) vs. "You can go ahead with the project." (informal)
"Might I suggest an alternative approach?" (very formal) vs. "Can I suggest something else?" (informal)
"Clients shall be notified in writing." (formal/legal) vs. "We'll let the clients know in writing." (informal)
"One must consider all options." (formal) vs. "You have to think about all the options." (informal)
📖 Reading Practice
The Future of Work

As technology continues to evolve, experts believe that the nature of work will change dramatically in the coming decades. Artificial intelligence and automation must be considered as significant factors that will transform various industries. Many routine jobs might disappear, while new roles that we cannot even imagine today will emerge.

"Workers will need to adapt continuously," explains Dr. Elena Rodriguez, a labor economist. "Those who can master new skills quickly should have better prospects. However, we must not forget that technological advancement can create opportunities as well as challenges."

Companies may need to restructure their operations entirely. Traditional office spaces could become less relevant as remote work becomes more common. "Organizations must embrace flexibility," says Carlos Mendes, a business strategist. "They should invest in digital infrastructure and would benefit from developing new management approaches."

Governments will have to reconsider education and social policies. "We ought to prepare the next generation for this new reality," argues Education Minister Paulo Silva. "Schools must focus more on creativity, critical thinking, and adaptability. Students should learn how to learn, as they might need to change careers multiple times throughout their lives."

While these changes may seem daunting, they need not be viewed negatively. With proper planning and adaptation, society could create a future where work becomes more fulfilling and better aligned with human potential.
Questions:
According to the text, what factors will influence the future of work?
What skills might be important for workers in the future?
Identify five different modal verbs used in the text and explain their functions.
✏️ Practice Exercises
📘 Practice 1 - Modal Verb Function Identification
Identify the function of the modal verb in each sentence (ability, possibility, permission, obligation, advice, etc.):
You must submit your application before the deadline.
She can play the piano beautifully.
We might go to the beach this weekend, depending on the weather.
May I borrow your dictionary?
You should see a doctor about that persistent cough.
The package will arrive tomorrow.
Would you mind opening the window?
The suspect must have left the scene before the police arrived.
📘 Practice 2 - Modal Verb Selection
Choose the most appropriate modal verb to complete each sentence:
You _______ (should/would/might) take an umbrella. The weather forecast predicts rain.
_______ (Can/Must/Would) you help me with these bags, please?
You _______ (must/should/might) not enter this area without proper authorization.
She _______ (will/would/used to) visit her grandparents every summer when she was a child.
This _______ (can/could/must) be the solution to our problem.
I _______ (may/will/should) call you tomorrow to discuss the details.
They _______ (must/can/might) be at home now, but I'm not certain.
You _______ (need/should/would) to have informed me earlier about the change in plans.
📘 Practice 3 - Sentence Transformation
Rewrite these sentences using the modal verb indicated in parentheses:
I'm sure she is at home now. (must)
I advise you to study harder. (should)
It's possible that they will join us later. (might)
Do you have the ability to speak Spanish? (can)
Is it OK if I use your phone? (may)
It's necessary for you to complete this form. (have to)
I'm certain he didn't steal the money. (can't)
What's your prediction about the election results? (will)
📘 Practice 4 - Translation Challenge
Translate these Portuguese sentences into English, paying special attention to modal verbs:
Você deve entregar o relatório até sexta-feira.
Ela pode falar cinco idiomas fluentemente.
Posso usar seu computador por um momento?
Você não deveria comer tantos doces.
Eles devem estar em casa agora.
Você tem que chegar cedo amanhã.
Eu poderia ter estudado mais para o exame.
Você gostaria de jantar conosco esta noite?
🔁 Deep Review
Modal verbs are essential tools for expressing nuanced meanings related to ability, possibility, permission, obligation, and more. Here's a summary of key points:
Modal verbs don't change form for different subjects and are followed by the base form of the main verb without "to"
Each modal verb can express multiple meanings depending on context
Can/could express ability, possibility, and permission
May/might express formal permission and possibility
Shall/should express suggestions, future plans, advice, and expectations
Will/would express future actions, predictions, promises, willingness, and hypothetical situations
Must/have to express strong obligation, necessity, and logical deduction
Modal combinations with perfect and continuous infinitives express complex meanings about time and aspect
Modal verbs often change in reported speech
Quick Review Questions:
What's the difference between "must" and "have to" when expressing obligation?
How do "may" and "might" differ in terms of expressing possibility?
When would you use "could have done" versus "should have done"?
How do you express prohibition using modal verbs?
🏠 Homework
📅 Day 1 - Writing

Write a formal email (200-250 words) to a professor requesting an extension for an assignment. Use at least six different modal verbs appropriately. Underline each modal verb and briefly explain its function in parentheses.
📅 Day 2 - Listening
Watch this TED Talk: "The surprising habits of original thinkers" by Adam Grant (
https://www.ted.com/talks/adam_grant_the_surprising_habits_of_original_thinkers
). Make notes of five different uses of modal verbs you hear. For each one, write down the complete sentence and explain why that particular modal verb was used in that context.
📅 Day 3 - Grammar
Rewrite these sentences using the appropriate modal verb or modal combination:
I'm sure she is the best candidate for the position. (must)
It was unnecessary for you to buy so much food. (needn't)
I'm certain he didn't reveal the secret. (can't)
I advise you to start saving for retirement early. (should)
Perhaps we will go to the theater this weekend. (might)
Do you have the ability to solve this equation? (can)
I regret not studying medicine. (could)
It's possible that he was working late last night. (may)
📅 Day 4 - Speaking
Record yourself responding to these scenarios, using appropriate modal verbs:
Give advice to a friend who is experiencing work-related stress.
Make predictions about how technology will change education in the next decade.
Express uncertainty about your plans for the weekend.
Discuss obligations you have at work or school.
Talk about abilities you had as a child but have lost as an adult. Listen to your recording and note any errors in your use of modal verbs.
📅 Day 5 - Vocabulary/Context
Create a dialogue between a career counselor and a client seeking advice about changing careers. The dialogue should be 12-15 exchanges long and include at least:
2 expressions of ability
2 expressions of possibility
2 expressions of advice
2 expressions of obligation
1 expression of prohibition
1 expression of logical deduction
📅 Day 6 - Creativity/Reflection
Choose one option:
Write a short story (250-300 words) about a character facing a difficult decision. Use modal verbs to express the character's thoughts about possibilities, obligations, and potential outcomes.

Write a reflection (250-300 words) on how modal verbs in English differ from similar expressions in Portuguese. Include specific examples of situations where the languages express modality differently and how this affects your understanding and use of English.
